title: AI-exposed college majors faced a weaker and lower-paid first job after ChatGPT
source_unit: CES-26-56 using Post-Secondary Employment Outcomes, American Community Survey occupation distributions, and Census Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics records
geography: United States; participating institutions in 24 states and 27 data partners, with LEHD outcomes excluding Alaska and Michigan

observations.period: Bachelor's graduates from 2016-2024; labor-market outcomes observed through 2025; paper published September 2026

denominator.unit: rounded graduate records in the filtered PSEO sample

initial_employment.value: The top decile of majors ranked by pre-period AI exposure had an approximately 5 percentage-point lower likelihood of employment in the quarter after graduation relative to the least-exposed comparison group after regression adjustment

initial_earnings.value: Full-quarter earnings about two quarters after graduation were approximately 13% lower for the top AI-exposure decile relative to the least-exposed comparison group

sectoral_reallocation.value: About half of the top-decile earnings decline was attributed to movement from higher-paying Information and Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services toward lower-paying Retail Trade and Accommodation and Food Services

longer_horizon.value: Effects attenuated as graduates moved farther from entry, but the top exposure decile still had lower employment and earnings estimates about two years after graduation

ai_exposure.value: Exposure was assigned before outcomes from occupation-task exposure measures mapped to major-level occupation distributions; it is not a direct measure of each employer's adoption or each worker's actual AI use

observations.method: The paper uses an event-time design comparing graduates from college majors with different pre-period AI exposure around the late-2022 public release of ChatGPT, with institution-major, institution-quarter, and major-quarter-of-year controls. Employment, earnings, employer, industry, and job-switching outcomes come from linked administrative records.
observations.uncertainty: The study is a Census CES working paper and not a Census Bureau endorsement. It covers about 29% of bachelor's degrees in the selected PSEO partner institutions, which are disproportionately public, urban, large, and research-oriented. The post-ChatGPT window is short, exposure measures are snapshots, and other time-varying shocks cannot be fully ruled out. Employment means observed UI-covered employment, not all work or wellbeing.
observations.subgroup: Graduates are grouped by major-level AI exposure deciles, with especially large effects in computer science, information systems, and software-related fields; outcomes are also examined by industry, job switching, institution, and timing relative to graduation.
observations.counterinterpretation: The timing and concentration are consistent with an AI-related labor-demand shock, but the design does not isolate one mechanism. Reduced entry-level demand, employer screening, sector-specific conditions, graduate supply, remote work, delayed graduate school or self-employment, and other coincident shocks may contribute. Lower initial earnings do not by themselves establish long-run career scarring, household hardship, or political response.

boundary: This record adds a bounded technology-to-labor-market-entry pathway. It does not establish a national AI displacement rate, actual individual AI use, discrimination, long-run career loss, household security, or political and cultural change.
